title: Algebra to TMUA: a short diagnostic
author: Arij Asad
note: Eight original questions to help choose practice. This is not a TMUA mock, a complete syllabus assessment or a score predictor.

questions.title: Square roots and signs
questions.hint: Use \(\sqrt{u^2}=|u|\), then decide the sign of \(x-3\).
solution: The square root is non-negative, so \(\sqrt{(x-3)^2}=|x-3|\). Since \(x<3\), we have \(x-3<0\) and therefore \(|x-3|=-(x-3)\).
Hence \[\frac{\sqrt{(x-3)^2}}{x-3}=\frac{-(x-3)}{x-3}=-1.\] The denominator is non-zero because \(x<3\).
questions.misconception: Writing \(\sqrt{u^2}=u\) loses the sign information when \(u<0\).
followup_solution: Since \(x>4\), \(4-x<0\), so \(\sqrt{(4-x)^2}=|4-x|=x-4\). Dividing by the non-zero quantity \(x-4\) gives \(1\).

questions.title: Factorisation and domain
questions.prompt: Simplify \(\dfrac{x^3+27}{x^2-9}\), stating all excluded values of \(x\).
questions.hint: Record the zeros of the original denominator before using the sum-of-cubes identity.
solution: The original denominator is zero at \(x=3\) and \(x=-3\), so both values are excluded.
Factor the numerator and denominator: \[x^3+27=(x+3)(x^2-3x+9),\qquad x^2-9=(x+3)(x-3).\]
For permitted values, cancel the common factor \(x+3\). This gives \(\dfrac{x^2-3x+9}{x-3}\), with \(x\ne -3,3\). The cancellation does not restore \(x=-3\) to the original domain.
questions.misconception: A cancelled factor can remove a visible restriction from the formula, but it does not change the domain of the original expression.
followup_solution: The original denominator gives \(x\ne\pm5\). Factor \(x^3-125=(x-5)(x^2+5x+25)\) and \(x^2-25=(x-5)(x+5)\).
Cancel \(x-5\) for permitted values to obtain \(\dfrac{x^2+5x+25}{x+5}\), still with \(x\ne\pm5\).

questions.title: Rational inequalities
questions.hint: Move everything to one side and use a sign chart. Do not multiply by an expression whose sign you have not fixed.
solution: First exclude \(x=-2\). Subtracting \(2\) gives \[\frac{x-1}{x+2}-2=\frac{-x-5}{x+2}\geq0.\]

The critical values are \(-5\) and \(-2\). For \(x<-5\), the numerator is positive and the denominator negative. For \(-5<x<-2\), both are negative. For \(x>-2\), the numerator is negative and the denominator positive.
The fraction is non-negative on \([-5,-2)\). Include \(-5\), where the numerator is zero; exclude \(-2\), where the expression is undefined.
questions.misconception: Multiplying by \(x+2\) without considering its sign can reverse an inequality incorrectly or lose an entire interval.
followup_solution: With \(x\ne1\), rearrange to \(\dfrac{5-2x}{x-1}\leq0\). The critical values are \(1\) and \(5/2\).
The fraction is negative for \(x<1\), positive for \(1<x<5/2\), and negative for \(x>5/2\). Include \(5/2\), where the fraction is zero, and exclude \(1\).

questions.title: Combining conditions
questions.prompt: Find all real \(x\) such that \(x^2>9\) and \(x<1\).
questions.hint: Solve each condition separately, then take their intersection.
solution: The inequality \(x^2>9\) gives \(x<-3\) or \(x>3\). The second condition is \(x<1\).
Every value with \(x<-3\) satisfies \(x<1\), while no value with \(x>3\) does. Therefore the intersection is \(x<-3\).
questions.misconception: The word "and" requires both conditions. Squaring inequalities can also hide a negative branch.
questions.followup: Find all real \(x\) such that \(x^2\leq16\) and \(x>-1\).
followup_solution: The first condition gives \(-4\leq x\leq4\). Intersect this with \(x>-1\) to obtain \(-1<x\leq4\).

questions.title: Modulus equations
questions.hint: Split at \(x=1/2\), and keep the condition attached to each branch.
solution: If \(x\geq1/2\), then \(|2x-1|=2x-1\). Thus \(2x-1=x+2\), giving \(x=3\), which satisfies this branch condition.
If \(x<1/2\), then \(|2x-1|=1-2x\). Thus \(1-2x=x+2\), giving \(x=-1/3\), which also satisfies its branch condition.
Both values satisfy the original equation, so the complete solution set is \(\{-1/3,3\}\).
questions.misconception: Using both signs without checking branch conditions can admit values that do not satisfy the original equation.
followup_solution: Both values meet their branch conditions and satisfy the original equation.

questions.title: Graphs and transformed inputs
questions.prompt: The graph of a quadratic \(f\) opens upwards and has roots \(-2\) and \(4\). Given \(f(0)<0\), find all \(x\) for which \(f(2x-1)<0\).
questions.hint: Find which inputs make \(f\) negative, then put \(2x-1\) between those inputs.
solution: An upward-opening quadratic is negative strictly between its roots, so \(f(t)<0\) exactly when \(-2<t<4\).
Use \(t=2x-1\): \[-2<2x-1<4\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -1<2x<5\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad-\frac12<x<\frac52.\]
The endpoints are excluded because the quadratic is zero there. The condition \(f(0)<0\) agrees with the sign of the graph between its roots.
questions.misconception: Changing the input of a function requires solving for the new variable; the original root interval cannot simply be reused.
questions.followup: A quadratic \(g\) opens upwards and has roots \(1\) and \(7\). Find all \(x\) such that \(g(3x+1)>0\).
followup_solution: The function is positive outside its roots: \(g(t)>0\) when \(t<1\) or \(t>7\). Thus \(3x+1<1\) or \(3x+1>7\), giving \(x<0\) or \(x>2\).

questions.title: Using identities efficiently
questions.prompt: A positive real number \(x\) satisfies \(x+1/x=4\). Find \((x-1/x)^2\).
questions.hint: Compare the expansions of the sum squared and the difference squared.
solution: The second expression is four less than the first. Hence \[(x-1/x)^2=(x+1/x)^2-4=16-4=12.\] There is no need to solve a quadratic for \(x\).
questions.misconception: The middle term of a square matters: \((a-b)^2\) is not \(a^2-b^2\).
questions.followup: A positive real number \(x\) satisfies \(x+1/x=5\). Find \((x-1/x)^2\).

questions.title: Counting distinct roots
questions.prompt: For which values of \(k>0\) does \(|x^2-4|=k\) have exactly two distinct real solutions?
questions.hint: Rewrite the equation as two equations for \(x^2\), and check the point where one right-hand side becomes zero.
solution: The equation is equivalent to \(x^2=4+k\) or \(x^2=4-k\). Since \(k>0\), the first equation always has two distinct real roots.
When \(0<k<4\), the second equation also has two distinct non-zero roots. They differ from the first pair, so there are four roots in total.
When \(k=4\), the second equation gives only \(x=0\), so there are three distinct roots. When \(k>4\), it has no real roots, leaving exactly two.
questions.misconception: At a transition value, the two expressions \(+0\) and \(-0\) are the same root. Count distinct roots separately at the boundary.
questions.followup: For which values of \(k>0\) does \(|x^2-9|=k\) have exactly three distinct real solutions?
followup_solution: The equations are \(x^2=9+k\) and \(x^2=9-k\). For \(0<k<9\) there are four distinct roots; for \(k>9\) there are two.
At \(k=9\), the roots are \(x=0\) and \(x=\pm\sqrt{18}=\pm3\sqrt2\). These are three distinct real roots, so \(k=9\) is the only value.
